newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania Socialist PM says election was democratic.
newsitem.headline: Albania Socialist PM says election was democratic.

text.p: Albania's interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, whose Socialist Party claimed victory in a general election, said on Monday the poll was democratic and he urged Albanians to work towards securing peace in the country.
Official results have yet to be announced and it is impossible to forecast the outcome of Sunday's election which was seen as a first step to restoring order after months of violence and unrest.
President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party, in power since 1992, insists it is far too early for any party to triumph but has acknowledged that it may not have won as many seats as it had expected.

"The elections on June 29 took place in a quiet, democratic and peaceful climate," Fino said in an address on state television. "I thank all the Albanian people from north to south for showing great national responsibility in turning out to vote massively and making a precious contribution for the future of democracy in Albania."

Fino, who took office in March when a 10-party unity coalition was formed to halt the spreading choas, appealed to police and state officials to work responsibly. More than 1,500 people have been killed in violence sparked by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes in January. The south still remains outside government control.

"I ask all officials of state, the police, army and national information service (the secret police), the republican guard, the courts and state prosecution to carry out their duties with responsibility," he added.
Albania was calm in the hours following the bitterly-contested general election and Tirana citizens heeded warnings by the Interior Ministry not to stage celebrations in the capital on Sunday night.

Socialist Party supporters celebrated outside their party's headquarters and some youths raced around the city in cars hanging flags out of windows, but the revelry was not as widespread or noisy as the jubilation seen after last year's disputed general election.
The Democrats won most parliamentary seats in the 1996 poll which was criticised by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) as seriously flawed.

The OSCE, together with the Council of Europe and a 100-strong delegation from the United States monitored Sunday's first round of the election and appeared broadly satisfied with the conduct of the poll.

OSCE election certification officer Catherine Lalumiere was due to announce the preliminary findings of around 500 international observers, who monitored voting around the country under the guard of a 7,000-strong multinational protection force.

Socialist leader Fatos Nano, released from jail in March three years after what was widely considered a suspect trial, said on Sunday night his party's data showed it had won 60 of 115 seats contested under majority voting in Sunday's election.

With expectations of gaining at least half the remaining 40 seats shared out under a proportional system, Nano said the Socialists and allied leftist parties would hold a two-thirds majority in parliament.
A two-thirds majority would be enough to remove Berisha by parliamentary vote. The president insists he will respect the election but said he would be unable to work with a leftist administration.

Albanians were also asked to vote in a referendum on whether to replace the republic with a constitutional monarchy. The monarchist party on Monday claimed they had clinched a majority of votes around the country, enabling Leka, son of Zog, Albania's king from 1928 to 1939, to assume the throne.
But the central electoral commission said they were unable so far to announce any results from the referendum.

The commission appealed to regional electoral centres to try to send result lists to central headquarters in Tirana by 6 p.m. (1600 GMT) but communications are difficult in this Balkan state which was isolated by its Stalinist regime for more than 40 years until communism was toppled in 1990.
